title: Fayum Portrait of a Man
description: A painted wood mummy portrait of a bearded man wearing a gold laurel wreath, from the Fayum region of Roman Egypt — the same broad Egyptian visual culture, in the same century, that produced Alexandria's teachers and seekers.
repository: Brooklyn Museum (Open Collection, via Internet Archive mirror)
licenseNotes: Verified directly: the archive.org item's own metadata record links to the Brooklyn Museum's rights statement, which reads exactly 'No known copyright restrictions' — one of the license categories the sourcing brief explicitly names as acceptable. Fetched and confirmed in this session.
notes: Two honest caveats: (1) this is a Fayum portrait — Fayum is a different region of Egypt from Alexandria itself, though part of the same Roman-Egyptian milieu and century; it depicts an anonymous private individual, not a named Christian teacher or a scene from the catechetical school. (2) Brooklyn's own scan is only 371x768px — no higher-resolution file exists in this item on Internet Archive, so it was NOT upscaled to the usual ~1600px target; it will look softer than the other approved images if used at large size. Chosen after an extensive second search (Cleveland + Brooklyn museum mirrors, ~15 additional query terms: origen, alexandria, logos, coptic, athanasius, clement, arius, serapis, papyrus, scroll, teacher+pupil, fayum, mummy portrait, roman egypt, encaustic) turned up nothing closer to a literal depiction of Alexandrian Christianity itself. SECOND SEARCH PASS (Opus-flagged as weak, redo requested): ~25 additional query terms tried across Cleveland, Brooklyn, and general Internet Archive image search (origen, alexandria, serapis, papyrus, reading+scroll, teacher+pupil, kom+el+shoqafa, catacombs+alexandria, plan+of+alexandria, etc). Found real leads only on the unreliable 'endlos' bulk-reupload account (self-declared licenses, no verifiable rights chain, boilerplate YouTube-scraped descriptions - excluded as not a reputable source) and a NASA satellite photo (no historical content). No better verified option found. This image's flaws stand as the review described: right general century-ish, wrong region (Fayum not Alexandria), slightly wrong date (just before the world's window), and wrong religion (a pagan funerary object, not neutral). Left in place for lack of a verified alternative - flagging for Mark that this one may be better left without a downloaded image than kept, given how directly it invites a false 'this is a picture of a Christian teacher' inference.

title: Drachm: Bust of Hormizd II (obverse)
description: Silver drachm bearing the crowned bust of Hormizd II, Sasanian king of Persia (r. 303-309 CE) — the immediate predecessor and father of Shapur II, whose later persecution took the bishop Simeon bar Sabbae and emptied the Persian church's chief see for twenty years.
repository: The Cleveland Museum of Art (Open Access, via Internet Archive mirror)
licenseNotes: Verified directly: the archive.org item's own metadata record for this Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access object carries licenseurl https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ (CC0), fetched and confirmed in this session.
notes: Honest caveat: this coin depicts Hormizd II, not Shapur II himself (Cleveland's Sasanian numismatic holdings jump from Hormizd II straight to much later Byzantine emperors, with no Shapur II coin found) — but it is the same dynasty, one reign earlier, squarely within this world's persecution-era timeframe, and a genuine dateable 4th-century Sasanian royal portrait rather than a later artistic imagining. Chosen after an extensive second search across Cleveland + Brooklyn mirrors (ephrem, nestorius, sassanian, persian king, zoroastrian, shapur, sasanian king, drachm king, julian, valens — the last two tried because Cleveland's coin collection was the most promising lead) turned up no closer match; a portrait bust coin of Shapur II himself, or an image of Edessa/Nisibis directly, would be a stronger swap if a reviewer finds one with a normal, unrestricted connection. REJECTED on second review pass (Opus): illustrates the wrong king (not the persecutor named in the tile), and Hormizd II is not himself remembered as a persecutor at all - the coin carries no Christian, Syriac, Edessene, or Nisibene content whatsoever. Replaced by syr-mar-shimoun-patriarch-badger1852.

title: Rock-cut cave churches, Göreme Open Air Museum
depictedPeriod: landscape and rock-cut monastic complex, occupied and carved mainly 4th-13th centuries CE
description: A daylight landscape photograph of the volcanic-tuff cliffs at the Göreme Open Air Museum in Cappadocia, showing the carved window and door openings of the rock-cut cave churches and monastic cells that riddle the rock face.
licenseNotes: Verified directly: the archive.org item's own metadata record carries licenseurl http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/, fetched and confirmed in this session. Attribution required (photographer: Ferah Kaya) - unlike the CC0 picks used for the other worlds, any use of this image should credit the photographer.
notes: Approved by Mark as a deliberately looser-bar exception for this one world: after two exhaustive search passes (70+ query terms across the Cleveland and Brooklyn museum Open Access mirrors) found no image of Basil, the Gregorys, or Macrina in any CC0/unambiguous-PD collection reachable from this sandbox, Mark approved using a modern, attribution-required photo of Cappadocia's cave-monastery landscape instead of leaving this world's approved slot empty. This is a landscape/architecture photo, not a portrait of a named figure - it establishes the physical setting (rock-cut monastic cells and churches) rather than depicting Basil's brotherhoods directly. Cropped to remove a strip of modern cafeteria signage at the bottom edge of the original tourist photo; otherwise unedited. The original item contains 8 more photos from the same visit (interior shots, UNESCO plaques, museum signage) if a reviewer wants an alternate crop or angle. SECOND PASS FIX (Opus review): the original crop still showed a streetlamp, paved walkway, and power lines in the bottom third, reading as a tourist snapshot. Re-cropped much tighter to just the cliff face and sky (top ~63% of the original photo) - no modern intrusions remain. The 8 companion photos from the same shoot were also checked; all had more, not less, modern infrastructure in frame (shop roofs, satellite dishes), so this remains the best of the set.

title: Mar Shimoun, Patriarch of the Nestorians
depictedPeriod: the Patriarchate (Mar Shimoun) is a continuous office traceable to the Church of the East this world describes; this specific Patriarch held office in the 1840s
artworkDate: 1852 lithograph by F. C. Cooper, published in G. P. Badger's 'The Nestorians and their Rituals'
description: A lithographed portrait of Mar Shimoun, 19th-century Patriarch of the Church of the East (the 'Nestorian' church) — the direct continuing lineage of the East Syriac Christianity this world describes — shown holding a bishop's crosier.
repository: Internet Archive (scan of G. P. Badger, The Nestorians and their Rituals, vol. II, London: Joseph Masters, 1852)
licenseNotes: Confirmed directly: published 1852 (author George Percy Badger died 1888), safely public domain in the US as a pre-1929 publication. Fetched and page-located directly from Internet Archive in this session.
notes: Replaces the rejected Hormizd II coin after a second review pass. This is NOT a 4th-5th century image - it is an 1852 portrait of the Patriarch of the same church (the 'Church of the East'/'Nestorian' church) many centuries later, the closest verifiable link to this world's actual institution (the tile's own question of whether authority rested more in the covenant-vow or 'in a bishop's office' is literally what the crosier signifies). No image from the world's own 200-410 CE window survives or was found in any collection reachable this session. Caption should say plainly: this is the same church's Patriarch, photographed/drawn 1400+ years later, not a contemporary image. Located by tracing the book's own preface ('the two views of an old Nestorian church contained in the second volume') to volume II, where the portrait appears as an early plate; the book also depicts other regional religious leaders (a Yezidi sheikh appears in volume I) so any further plates pulled from this source should be double-checked for which community they actually depict before use.
